sections.title: Name and identification
sections.text: Infundibulicybe geotropa (trooping funnel, monk’s head), long known as Clitocybe geotropa, is a large mushroom with a cream, buff or pale ochre cap. The cap is often 10–15 cm across and sometimes about 20–25 cm in descriptions. It starts convex with a central boss and inrolled margin, then spreads and becomes funnel-shaped, often retaining the boss. Surface smooth and matt.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The gills are crowded, cream to pale ochre, and deeply decurrent down the stem. The stem is long (about 10–30 cm in some descriptions), sturdy, cylindrical to slightly club-shaped, fibrous, smooth and ringless; the base may be swollen. Flesh white, thick and firm, especially when young. Smell described as sweet, sometimes like bitter almonds; sources differ on its strength. Spore print white.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: Grows on soil, especially in broadleaf woods, clearings and edges, hedgerows and nearby grassy places; also reported in conifer woods. Fruiting bodies often grow in rows, arcs or rings. Fruiting is mainly in autumn, sometimes from August into early winter depending on region.

sections.title: Lookalikes and caution
sections.text: Its large size, persistent central boss and strongly decurrent gills are useful clues, but do not identify a collection on their own. The poisonous livid pinkgill (Entoloma sinuatum) can be mistaken for pale mushrooms: its gills are sinuate rather than decurrent and its spore print is pink. The miller (Clitopilus prunulus) also has a pink spore print. The German DGfM lists this species among edible mushrooms and the Swiss VAPKO recommends it; these lists do not verify a specimen or its safety to eat. Do not eat a collection identified from a photo; seek expert confirmation.

traits: Cream to buff or pale ochre cap, often 10–15 cm and sometimes near 20–25 cm; convex then funnel-shaped, often retaining a central boss
Crowded, cream to pale ochre gills, deeply decurrent down the stem
Long, sturdy, cylindrical to slightly club-shaped, fibrous stem without a ring; base sometimes swollen
White, thick, firm flesh, especially when young; sweet smell sometimes like bitter almond; white spore print
On soil in woods, clearings, edges, hedgerows or grassy places; often in rows, arcs or rings; mainly in autumn
safetyNote: The German DGfM includes Infundibulicybe geotropa on its positive list and the Swiss VAPKO recommends it, but neither verifies an individual specimen. The poisonous livid pinkgill (Entoloma sinuatum) can be confused with pale mushrooms; the miller also has a pink spore print. Do not eat a mushroom identified only from this entry or an image; seek expert confirmation. If ingestion is uncertain or symptoms occur, contact a poison centre or medical service promptly.
